MR. PERRON-REQUEST FOR FRENCH COPY OF PENSION COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. My question of privilege arises from the fact the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss La-Marsh) misled the house, intentionally or unintentionally, at yesterday's sitting. On the orders of the day, I directed the following question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson):
Can he tell the house whether there is any special reason why the French version of the report of the special joint committee which studied Bill No. C-136 during 51 sittings is not yet distributed, when we are almost through with that measure?
The Prime Minister answered as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think this comes within my responsibilities, but I will be glad to look into the matter.
The house again in committee, I directed the following question to the minister, as reported on page 11887 of Hansard:
Furthermore, as I pointed out, we do not have the French version of the report dealing with the study made by the committee where some of us brought forth our suggestions.
The minister answered as follows, as reported on page 11888 of Hansard:
I should like to say, however, that if the report of the pension committee to which my hon. friend has referred is the report of the special committee on the Canada pension plan, it has been reported in both French and in English and circulated to all hon. members.
I maintain that the said committee reports have not been printed in French or, at least, have not been circulated to all hon. members, for I have here a reply from an employee of the distribution section who wrote to me as follows yesterday:
The French version of the report of that committee has not yet been received. We have only received No. 1 concerning sittings of November 24, 25 and 26.
I would therefore ask the minister, if her statement is correct, to send us the French
20220-754J
version of all committee reports before consideration in committee of the pension plan is resumed. If she made a wrong statement yesterday, I would ask her to make the necessary correction.
Mr. Speaker, I maintain that if we do not have those committee reports in our own language while we are considering this bill, we do not have in our hands the necessary and essential implements for such consideration, and are thus greatly handicapped.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I move, seconded by Mr. Starr, the adjournment of the house in accordance with standing order No. 26 in order to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, namely the great alarm in all parts of Canada resulting from slack or careless administration of justice and law enforcement by the present government, which requires immediate investigation and the broadening of the terms of reference of the Dorion inquiry to include an examination of all the sinister circumstances surrounding the disappearance of an international narcotics criminal, Lucien Rivard.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
May I call upon the right hon. gentleman to discuss the urgency of this motion.
Administration of Justice

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the events are most recent. They have to do with the escape of Rivard last evening. So far as the administration of justice is concerned I say at once it falls within the jurisdiction of the province, but Rivard is in a particular position vis-a-vis the government of Canada. His extradition had been sought. He had been placed in this jail in Montreal to be held on behalf of the federal government until the determination of such proceedings as might be taken to prevent or accelerate his delivery to the United States.
It is not a question of criticism of the provincial authorities in any way. They were simply asked to keep custody of this person and to ensure that he was made available whenever his presence was required. In other words there is a responsibility resting on the Department of Justice. Rivard was their prisoner and they apparently did nothing to assure that this man, who had apparently exhausted every legal means to escape his responsibility to the law, was unable to take recourse to an escape from the jail. There was apparently no effort made by the Department of Justice to ensure that this man would be made available, and what has happened has resulted from a fantastic, even disgraceful caricature. People in the United States have always felt that the administration of justice in Canada was pure and undefiled.
I am not going into the evidence delivered before the Dorion commission, but from that we know this man tried every other means, and finally he chose a more direct means.
The federal government had a responsibility. They exercised it in so negligent a way that one of the worst criminals-and I say that if he is guilty of the offences charged against him in connection with narcotics- is free-

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Oh.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Are there still some over there who believe in this man?

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Now we have two ministers joining the others over there who were interested in this matter. I say that this house and Canada have a right to know what took place here. It is urgent; it is necessary if Canada's high standards of justice are to be upheld. There is no other means by which this matter can be brought before the house; this is the only way in which it can be done.

Administration of Justice I say there is no higher degree of urgency than attaches to the maintenance of unpolluted justice; and in all the circumstances of this case an unsavoury mess has been revealed.

He then went on to say-and I quote him because I wrote down his words-"I say at once the administration of justice falls within the jurisdiction of the province."
That being so, the right hon. gentleman was in fact telling you, Mr. Speaker, that he had no right to make a motion because it related exclusively to the escape of one Rivard from a jail which is not within the jurisdiction of this parliament or of the federal authority.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I recognize that Your Honour very seldom permits one of these motions for an adjournment, and under the circumstances that is understandable. However, I make a special appeal to Your Honour today on this particular motion because I am convinced that the people of Canada are perturbed and concerned about recent events.
I submit to Your Honour that this concern will not be removed merely by some questions on the orders of the day. The only way the minds of the Canadian people can be set at rest with reference to the Department of Justice and the conduct of the R.C.M.P. is by a full debate in this house in which ministers of the crown can state the facts and tell the people and the members of this house what has happened, so that


members in all parts of the house will be given the opportunity to ask questions and take part in the debate.
The President of the Privy Council has based his whole argument against the urgency of debate on the contention that this matter falls exclusively within provincial jurisdiction. I say, Mr. Speaker, that is a fallacious argument, and I say that for two reasons. The first is that Rivard was being held at the request of the federal government under extradition proceedings, he being wanted in the United States to face charges of dope smuggling. Surely this is a matter of federal jurisdiction. Surely this is something about which the federal government should be concerned. It is the federal Department of Justice who has a responsibility to the government of the United States to produce this man, not the government of Quebec. While it may be true that the province of Quebec had him in custody, they were holding him for the federal Department of Justice.
Under the circumstances I submit that this house has a right to know from the Minister of Justice what special security measures if any, were taken to make sure that this man would not escape. Particularly in view of the fact that evidence has been produced in recent weeks to show that this man was endeavouring to obtain bail, that he was prepared to jump bail, and that he had established bank accounts in various parts of the world to which he might go if he escaped from this country. All of this made it extremely important that special security measures should be invoked to make sure this man was kept in custody. We have the right, as has the country, to know whether the Minister of Justice and the R.C.M.P. instituted such special security measures.
The second thing we have a right to know, Mr. Speaker, is, what action was taken by the Minister of Justice and the R.C.M. Police to alert all detachments of the R.C.M.P. in various parts of Canada regarding this man's escape? At one o'clock today from Toronto the C.B.C. made the following announcement:
The escape last night was unknown to the police in metropolitan Toronto for almost four hours. The R.C.M.P. detachment in Toronto learned unofficially of the jail break at 9.30 p.m. when it was flashed on television two and a half hours after the escape. Police officials said the time lapse would have allowed Rivard to fly to Toronto and emplane there for almost any international point.
If that statement is true, Mr. Speaker, then this house has a right to an explanation from the Minister of Justice as to why, when an important person wanted in the United States

for dope smuggling breaks from jail, an alarm is not sent out to all points immediately in order that police might be on the lookout for him. If it is true that they were not notified officially for four hours and that they did not learn even unofficially of his escape for two and a half hours, then there has been, as this motion suggests, lax and careless administration of justice and law enforcement by the present government.
I express the hope, Mr. Speaker, that instead of the government arguing against urgency, the Prime Minister will rise and say that he welcomes a debate on the subject owing to the public concern which he must know is being felt from one end of Canada to the other. Because, Mr. Speaker, if Your Honour does not allow this debate and the government opposes the debate there will be a question left in the minds of the Canadian people regarding the lack of special security measures and failure to take prompt steps to make sure that this man was apprehended immediately after his escape. I think no one can sum it up better than the premier of the province of Quebec, Mr. Lesage, who said "There's something screwy here".

That happens quite often. When someone is charged with murder, he is put somewhere under the jurisdiction of the federal government and before he is to be hanged, he is taken to a provincial jail and brought back to Bordeaux.
A few months ago we witnessed the escape of the Sefkind brothers who managed a bankruptcy amounting to several millions of dollars. subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Once more, Mr. Speaker, we have heard that endless series of questions which, of course, do not call for any answer, because the one who asks them knows himself that no answer can be given to his questions because they correspond only to insinuations, innuendoes or completely unfair explanations.
The Leader of the Opposition has not told us and will not tell us, you can be sure, with respect to the detention of Rivard, which obligation or responsibility the Minister of Justice of Canada, the police or the federal government had. Finally, we will never get an answer to this question, because the Leader of the Opposition knows that in this case, as far as Rivard's detention and escape are concerned, there cannot be, neither legally nor in fact, any federal responsibility whatsoever.
Now, I do not want my words to be interpreted as suggesting that the provincial government did not discharge its own responsibilities. I am dealing with jurisdiction, and my words should not be distorted to suggest directly or indirectly that I made an accusation or some implication as regards the discharge of his duties by the attorney general of the province of Quebec. No, I deny it even before anybody attempts to insinuate that.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Who is responsible?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we will know who is responsible when the attorney general of the province of Quebec has completed his inquiry in respect to the circumstances of the escape. Only then can we know exactly if any responsibility can be attributed to someone and to whom-but not before then.
Mr. Speaker, the person who claims that he proclaimed the bill of rights is the first one who is endeavouring, since several months, to pass a judgment without taking facts into consideration, and to condemn before the courts have even rendered a Judgment. What good is a bill of rights, tens of thousands of copies of which were distributed under the signature of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, if this leads to the kind of situation we have today, to speeches such as those we heard a while ago?

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: This is poor.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: There has been an insinuation to the effect that Rivard has been pampered while in prison, that Rivard since his first arrest and detention has been pampered, that Rivard's extradition has been delayed in undue fashion. This is one more of those charges which, made in fact for political purposes-

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Tell that to the United States authorities.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: -and I say right away they are ill founded-constitute an unfair and unjust indictment and charge against judges who are not present in this chamber, against persons charged with the administration of justice who are not present in this chamber.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Sheer nonsense.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman wants the facts. He must remember that Rivard's extradition, which was requested in June of last year, was followed by committal for extradition by a judge of the Quebec superior court in September of last year. This, of course, was of no importance to the right hon. gentleman and he did not care to advise the house of it. These are the facts. Why did he not tell the House of Commons? Why did he have to hide these things?

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Why the $20,000 offer?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Another thing he forgot to tell the house, even though it is of some importance that we know the truth so that the facts may not be distorted and even though it is also a matter of public record, is that Rivard brought a habeas corpus application, which application was dismissed on January 29, 1965. Was Rivard pampered? Will the right hon. gentleman suggest that the Department of Justice had anything to do with the matter while the case was under advisement? Will he suggest-I deny it at once-that the judge who had the case under advisement intended to pamper Rivard in any way or to give him some preference and that the judge was in a conspiracy with the Department of Justice to do so?

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Why did it take nine months?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Of course he did not like to tell the house, because it would go in the press and the people of Canada might find out.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Lamontagne said he was offered $20,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: On February 11 of this year Rivard, the pampered criminal, the person who is supposed to have been pampered by the Department of Justice, made a further application by way of habeas corpus to a judge of the Quebec court of appeal. Judgment on this application was reserved, not by the Department of Justice, not by the government of Canada but by a duly constituted Canadian court, a court which, whether or not the right hon. gentleman likes it, followed the due process of law. To make the record complete-

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: He got away.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
-it must be added that at the time of Rivard's escape judgment had not been delivered in the second application for habeas corpus, so it cannot be said that I knew about the judgment. These are the facts, Mr. Speaker, and I say that with these facts in mind the right hon. gentleman, if he has a minimum of a sense of justice at all left in him, if he knows what the bill of rights means, should withdraw what he said in his speech.
Now, I want to come back to this question of responsibility, Mr. Speaker, and the charge that we have allegedly failed to discharge that responsibility. If the right hon. gentleman cared just as much for his reputation as a lawyer, which he is, as for his popularity as a politician, he would have recalled that under the Penitentiary Act penitentiaries are institutions of detention for people sentenced to two years or more by a judge. Penitentiaries, under the act, are not used for the detention of persons for interim or short term custody. Furthermore, being a former prime minister of this country, a former head of the government, he should know that extradition prisoners are always held in provincial jails.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Held, how long?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Now, Mr. Speaker, under whose jurisdiction are provincial jails? In the province of Quebec, as in all the other provinces of Canada, they are, and it is nearly humiliating to have to repeat this to the right hon. gentleman, under provincial jurisdiction. More particularly, provincial jails in the province of Quebec, and here I am proud to agree with the right hon. gentleman, are under the jurisdiction of a man whom, I am proud to say, the right hon. gentleman described as follows a few minutes ago: "The attorney general of Quebec, both as a judge and as a minister, set an example that must be followed." Well, Mr. Speaker, in so far as the detention of a man detained in a provincial jail is concerned, if one relies on the discharge of his functions by an attorney general
Administration of Justice who, both as a judge and as a minister set an example that must be followed, is that, on the part of the Minister of Justice of Canada, failing to discharge his own responsibilities?

Mr. Speaker, I believe that it is high time in this chamber to stop using parliamentary immunity in order to make insinuations which cannot be justified by facts-

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: There is no insinuation; it was gross negligence on your part. [Translation]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: -to connect to a so-called sensational proposal a lot of unrelated circumstances, without saying whether or not the issue comes under the government, and to imply in a vague but obviously dangerous way that the government is responsible for the whole affair, that the situation is the result of some sinister plot hatched in the night by the Minister of Justice, members of the government, a certain criminal and all the judges in Quebec and Canada.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: What a fantasy.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Is that not what the right hon. Leader of the Opposition implied in the speech he has just made?
Still in this connection and as far as the discharge of our responsibilities is concerned, as soon as it learned of Rivard's and Du-rocher's escape yesterday, the government immediately took appropriate action to extend its fullest co-operation to provincial and municipal police authorities.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Too late.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must say that early in the evening-

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Too little, too late.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
-I got a phone call from the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) who, as a citizen, was at least as concerned about the matter as the Leader of the Opposition, believe me.
I immediately got in touch with the R.C.M.P. which had just heard the news. Photographs, for the purpose of identification, were being prepared to be distributed by the R.C.M.P. to all the police forces in Canada who would need them. Moreover, the R.C.M.P. was already contacting its detachments including those responsible for airports and all federal properties.
As for the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), he had, without loss of time,

Administration of Justice got in touch with the authorities of the two great crown corporations responsible for transportation. He also took the necessary steps so that every airport be informed and warned to check the flights in order to prevent, as far as possible, Rivard from taking a plane to proceed on his escape.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: May I interrupt the minister to ask him if he could tell us the hour at which the R.C.M.P. detachments were alerted and the hour at which railways and airports were alerted?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I can say, in all fairness, that this went on generally between nine and midnight last night. If I am not mistaken, the department was informed about nine o'clock.
Now, I have here a brief note written by my parliamentary secretary from a telephone call by Deputy Commissioner Bingham; it reads as follows:

That he, Assistant Commissioner Bingham, was notified at home at 8.35 p.m. by Assistant Commissioner Bordeleau of the Montreal detachment. Bingham ordered Bordeleau to get out an account of the facts and descriptions of the two men by telex at once. The Ottawa telex was received at 9.46 p.m. Any delay was due to preparation of descriptions, but when received by R.C.M.P. detachment this was in turn disseminated to all subdivisions and to local police authorities.
Bingham notified the F.B.I. liaison officer here and notified R.C.M.P. liaison in Washington for information of the bureau of narcotics. Files here in Ottawa were referred to and all available information on the two escapees prepared and sent out.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: What time was that?

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: May I ask the minister would he also give us the hour at which Rivard escaped? Is 7.20 the correct time?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: The matter was on the police telex at 9.46 p.m., and the right hon. gentleman and all members of the opposition may take for granted, in view of the manner in which this work was done, that the R.C.M.P. dealt with this matter in its usual efficient and rapid manner.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
May I repeat the question I asked the minister. Can he give us the official hour at which it is estimated Rivard escaped

from Bordeaux jail? I believe the newspapers said 7.20 p.m. Is that the correct time?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I told the house that the attorney general of Quebec was expected to make a report this afternoon. I have given instructions to obtain a copy of that report either by phone or telex. There were variations in the reports last night as to the exact hour or moment of the escape. I would much sooner rely on that report to determine for the purposes of the house exactly at what time the escape took place.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: May I ask a further question? Would the minister please inquire as to why it was that the R.C.M.P. telex message went out at 9.46 when I personally was able to hear the details of this thing on C.B.C.-F.M. network at about 9.12?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I said the R.C.M.P. was notified in Ottawa at 8.35 p.m. and the descriptions had been prepared and placed on the general telex at 9.46 p.m. I think this is not only pretty good but very efficient work.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Two hours and 20 minutes later.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: No, less than an hour.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Check your arithmetic.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is now quite clear that these same hon. gentlemen of the official opposition, who a few minutes ago were complaining about the fact that the R.C.M.P. was not sufficiently supported or maintained, are now those who decry the R.C.M.P. for having done its duty last night.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mind what you say, because that is going to bounce right back in your teeth.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: That is completely false.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Now, Mr. Speaker, I was going to add that during that period, between nine o'clock and let us say, eleven o'clock, but mostly between nine and ten o'clock, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration also had a conference with the director of immigration and instructions were given that all ports of entry be notified, that all immigration stations, including those at the airports, be notified and put on the alert, and that communication be established with the United States authorities.
All the resources of the R.C.M.P. are maintained at the disposal of all concerned for the purpose of determining the whereabouts of Rivard and of ensuring his arrest. Full co-ordination has been effected and estab-

lished between the R.C.M.P., the provincial police and the municipal police corps, and this house may be assured that so far as federal jurisdiction is concerned nothing has been, nothing will be and nothing is being left undone to ensure that the ends of justice be fully pursued and obtained.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I can only say, once and for all, because there must be a stop to this deliberate shifting of one's ground, that if the federal authorities took it upon themselves, either in the case of Rivard's custody or that of any person doing a term of less than two years in provincial jails, to intervene as far as their custody or their detention is concerned, it would be an encroachment- and the opposition knows it-upon the rights and responsibilities of the provinces under the Canadian constitution.
What is being implied, after all, is that the federal government should have surrounded Rivard's guards by men of its own. Probably the Leader of the Opposition would have wanted a cordon of provincial guards, then a cordon of federal law officers and finally a further cordon of international policemen which would watch over everyone.
In conclusion, I must say that, in the administration of justice, this government acts as honestly as the Leader of the Opposition did when he was at the head of the government. I feel I must repeat that, because the right hon. gentleman claims that we have made mistakes.

It is all very well to imply that this government has delayed in certain cases the administration of justice. But the Minister of Justice may have wanted to consider in certain cases whether or not it was desirable either to take proceedings or to lay an information.
I am not implying that there was any impropriety in their time when the same thing was done, because each time the attorney general of Canada decided either not to prosecute-

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Under whom you served.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I am proud to have served under him.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Who was prime minister then?

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Maybe, on the suggestion of a member of parliament, he was called upon
Administration of Justice to make up his mind that either a prosecution was not advisable because the ends of justice would not be served in the circumstances, or even that a charge, let us say for forgery, ought to be withdrawn.
He did so in what I think was the full discharge of his responsibility, and I do not intend to accuse the previous government of having failed in this responsibility or of having been dishonest toward the people of Canada by accepting that state of affairs. But we should demand that the same fairness of judgment should be exercised in our case as in their case. That is all.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: You cannot expect that from them.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: You might as well shut up.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I will call attention to one forgery case where a charge was made and a parallel case of conspiracy instituted-the case of Buddy Leeds. A letter dated August 17, 1960, was signed by Walter Dinsdale and it was subsequently filed and tabled in this house. It is addressed to the executive assistant to the minister of justice, Ottawa, Canada. It reads-and one will find on all sides personal convictions which lead to the discussion with the minister of justice-"Dear Jim-". The writer is addressing Mr. James McAuley, the executive assistant to the minister:
Re: Buddy Leeds
I have had an opportunity to catch up on local developments on the Buddy Leeds case. His lawyers are still convinced that the only possible charge against him is altering a few documents which were never used.
What is forgery if it is not altering documents for the purpose of their being used, even if they are not used? The letter goes on:
My own personal contacts with Buddy convince me that his part in immigration cases has been merely to assist his fellow Chinese citizens to bring in dependants within the terms of the regulations.
Because of his high standing in the community a petition is circulating on Buddy's behalf. The case has been remanded twice now. What would you suggest as the best solution to the dilemma?
If I were like the right hon. gentleman I would ask: What was the dilemma?

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Was he offered a $20,000 bribe?

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Ask Walter.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Oh, oh.

Administration of Justice

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The letter goes on:
Must it proceed to preliminary hearing? If so, there is every possibility it could be dismissed for lack of evidence.
These are words which we in this house should never forget and which the Leader of the Opposition should never forget-"there is every possibility it could be dismissed for lack of evidence".

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Are you making a charge?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I will proceed-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Would the minister permit a question? Is he making a charge or is he just smearing-

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Sit down.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Then we read this:
The whole episode has not served to enhance the government's reputation in these parts.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: It had nothing to do with dope smuggling.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Smuggling was the charge.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Then it says:
I hope the police haven't been too over zealous in this case.
The next sentence in the letter will show why he hoped the police would not be over zealous. He expresses it in these words:
We don't want to get the reputation of operating a police state.
Any advice you could offer would be greatly appreciated.
I do not know what advice was offered, but the charge has been withdrawn, one year later.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Good.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: There have been other cases. There have been a few; quite a few.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: You were the deputy at the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: You were the prime minister.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: You were the prime minister administering justice. You forgot it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Withdraw that remark.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition, who should know about government organization, tells me I was the deputy minister at that time. Whether I was the deputy or the assistant deputy changes nothing with regard to ministerial government and government responsibility.
[Mr. Monteith.l

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: That is why we think you should resign.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: There is one thing which is to my great satisfaction. No officer of the Department of Justice-and if I had to suffer for this I would maintain that standard which is not the one which the right hon. gentleman is now suggesting-will-

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The hon. gentleman spoke of my standards. Let me say to him that his and mine are not the same, and he has proved that today.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, as to behaviour in this house at least, I am happy with that admission that our standards are not the same.

I cannot do better than to point out once more that while Rivard was in jail pending his extradition, the government was right in respecting the constitution and then in depending on the administration of justice in the province of Quebec by the man who, I am proud to repeat it, was described a little earlier by the Leader of the Opposition as a public man who, while on the bench and since he became a minister, has set an example in every respect.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Is it not the fact that under the provisions of the Extradition Act the primary responsibility, and the ultimate responsibility, for the federal government to honour its obligations to the other contracting parties lies upon the government, and pursuant to section 25 of that act lies specifically upon the minister the duty to deliver the prisoner when asked for by the officers of the country demanding him?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: What does all this mean to the Liberal party's slush fund? That is the question in the minds of the Canadian people. How much did the Liberal party make out of this?

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret, first of all, that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) should have spent part of his speech on this occasion on making an attack on the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) for something that happened a long time ago. I do not think that is a subject matter in this discussion and I think the Minister of Justice does himself no good by calling the kettle black, if that is what he is trying to do.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the core of the minister's speech in this house appears to be this. In fact, I took down the exact words he used. He said that the federal authorities are neither legally nor in fact under any responsibility whatever in respect to the escape of Rivard. I want to suggest to this house and to the minister that he has misunderstood the scope of his responsibility in this matter. I want to suggest that both the law of the country and the extraordinary circumstances of this case imposed a special degree of responsibility upon the minister and his department; and I have yet to hear, from what the minister has said, what are the facts which enable us to determine whether or not that responsibility has been discharged.
Now, what is the nature of the responsibility according to our law? First of all it is perfectly clear that this man was arrested by reason of the Extradition Act, which was passed by this parliament. That act is based upon treaties with foreign countries and imposes an obligation upon this country to see that those who are suspected fugitive crimi-
Administration of Justice nals are made available to the administration of justice in other countries.
It is perfectly true, as the minister has said, that it is up to a judge of the court to determine whether a prima facie case exists. But I call to the attention of the minister section 19 of the Extradition Act, which reads as follows:
Where the judge commits a fugitive to prison, he shall, on such committal,
... (b) transmit to the Minister of Justice a certificate of the committal-
And so on. So that the statute requires the minister to be informed of a committal to jail.
I will not read all the other sections but I will make reference to the point made by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) to show the obligation existing under section 25. That section says:
Subject to this part, the Minister of Justice, upon the requisition of the foreign state, may, under his hand and seal, order a fugitive who has been committed for surrender to be surrendered to the person or persons who are, in his opinion, duly authorized to receive him in the name and on behalf of the foreign state-
It is perfectly true that the committal is to a provincial jail. It is also perfectly true, as the minister says, that the responsibility for custody then rests upon the authorities who administer that particular jail. But I suggest that there is the underlying authority of the Minister of Justice throughout, in cases which involve extradition, to interest himself in whether or not the conditions of custody are adequately carried out. I suggest that the circumstances in this particular case impose a special duty upon the minister.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what are the circumstances? The circumstances are that this man was connected, or alleged to be connected, with a dope ring of organized crime in America. I presume the minister knows that these people have tremendous funds. They are completely unscrupulous. They use methods of bribery, corruption and violence. They corrupt police officers, jailers, and where possible even politicians. It is not only that this man was therefore in a category very different to any ordinary criminal, but that he had resources and a background, as far as one knows. We are not condemning him now because we have not heard his case, but there was a prima facie case against him, as being connected with this sordid, sinister gang of international criminals. Therefore, I suggest there was special reason to be careful in this case.
What was the next reason? The next reason was that through evidence before the Dorion commission, the R.C.M.P. made known
11950	HOUSE OF
Administration of Justice that this man was desperate to escape extradition to the United States. As far as the prima facie evidence goes, at any rate, he did not even stop short of offering $20,000 to be given by a special assistant to the lawyer acting on behalf of the United States. The prima facie evidence is that this man had the money and was ready to produce it, and that whatever happened he was desperately anxious to avoid justice in the United States of America. Surely, Mr. Speaker, ordinary prudence would require in a case of this sort and under these special circumstances that some special steps be taken to make sure that this man did not escape from justice in this country.
The questions I wish to ask the minister are these. Were any special precautions regarding the custody of Rivard recommended to the authorities of the provincial jail? Were the provincial jail authorities warned of the likelihood of an attempt by this man to escape? Were the circumstances which I have outlined and which were known to this government brought to the attention of the jailers? Did the R.C.M.P. ever consider taking special precautions, and I am not talking about a cordon standing around watching to see whether the provincial men were doing their job. What I am suggesting is that the R.C.M.P. realizing the seriousness and the importance of this matter, might very well have offered co-operation to make sure that this especially dangerous criminal, under these special circumstances, did not become a fugitive from justice. Was the R.C.M.P. requested to offer that co-operation and was that co-operation given? Was anything done other than just relying, as the minister does, on the fact that there is supposed to be some provincial responsibility in this case? I suggest there was mixed responsibility, federal and provincial responsibility. Did the federal government discharge its obligations simply by sending him to a provincial jail? I will agree that in a normal case that might have been a perfectly reasonable course of action. Under different circumstances it might have been reasonable to send him to a provincial jail and rely on the provincial jail to use adequate precautions to keep him in custody.
But, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the particular facts of this case required some particular attention, and I wonder if such attention was given.
In concluding what I have to say about this matter, and I have no desire to detain the house much longer, I would suggest that the circumstances surrounding this case re-


quire an explanation. There is a disquiet in the country and I think the reason for this disquiet is that it seems sometimes that this government does not understand what it is dealing with when it is dealing with organized crime. This is not small-scale petty crime in respect of which ordinary methods are good enough. What I fear is that if the government appears to be incompetent in dealing with organized crime, Canada itself will appear to be incompetent I am not suggesting that all was not done by the minister that ought to have been done, or that all that ought to have been done was not done by the R.C.M.P., but unless the minister can explain to this house whether any special precautions or efforts were taken, or any special warnings given to the people dealing with this case, he will not have discharged the responsibilities that rest on the shoulders of federal officers who are responsible to the United States of America in matters of extradition, such as exist in this case. Do we want to become the laughingstock of the United States because we cannot detain criminals, especially of the type involved in things like dope rings?
Those are the matters which are disturbing the people of Canada, Mr. Speaker, and nothing I have heard as yet from the minister satisfies me that there has been an adequate answer.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot speak this afternoon with the authority of a member of the legal profession, but certain things in regard to this case are obvious to the general public, and I feel I must make use of this opportunity to emphasize this very tragic state of affairs which has allowed a criminal such as Lucien Rivard to escape, as he did, from Bordeaux jail. That state of affairs is similar to the tragic state of affairs which allowed a man such as Hal Banks to escape from this country at a time when he was under a cloud. He had been under that cloud for some considerable period of time. Something must be wrong when this sort of thing can happen.
How careless could the custodians of Bordeaux jail have been to permit such a man as Rivard and his companion to slug a single guard and go out either through five steel gates or over a 25-foot wall and gain their freedom? Certainly everyone in Canada was aware that these were hardened, dangerous and experienced criminals. We have only to read the Dorion commission inquiry reports to understand that Rivard would stop at nothing. He endeavoured to bribe his way

out of the situation he was in when he was wanted by the United States authorities, and having failed in that regard he then threatened the life, or had the life threatened of the man he attempted to bribe. That is public knowledge.
One need only look at the press account of what actually took place last night to appreciate the character of this man. He stopped a car and talked with the driver Mr. Bourgeois. He was suave enough to talk on an intimate basis with the man as they drove three miles over the streets of Montreal. Before he ordered the man out he gave him a two-dollar bill for taxi fare from that point to the man's place of employment, and promised that he would phone the man at his office within the hour to tell him where he would find his car. Mr. Bourgeois, the man who owned the car, arrived at his office where he had to do some overtime work, and about seven fifty, according to this report, he received a phone call from Lucien Rivard who stated that his car was located at Fleury and Montee St. Michel. At that point Mr. Bourgeois called the police.
We must only look slightly further to find that Rivard's wife had visited the jail yesterday, had requested and obtained $2,000 which had been placed in safekeeping there after having been found in the possession of Rivard when he was taken into custody last June 19.
I am surprised because of these circumstances, and I do not think the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) can just shrug his shoulders and say, "we have no responsibility" particularly in light of the questions which have been asked by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin).
One need only read a little more of this article which appears in today's Ottawa Journal to find out that there had been a battle at Bordeaux jail among five prisoners who had been drinking homebrew, which apparently they had made at the jail. The article states:
Among the prisoners who were transferred to cells in downtown Montreal was Robert Collin, charged with capital murder in the death last September of nightclub doorman Rocky Brunette. Also charged in the case is Robert Gignac, another witness in the Dorion inquiry.
These are some of the things that cause us to wonder just what is taking place. It is not good enough for the government and the Minister of Justice simply to shrug their shoulders and say this is a provincial responsibility. Certainly it is, but here is a man who is wanted on a matter that concerns the fed-
Administration of Justice eral government and which involves most serious charges.
So I say it is imperative at this point that all of our security forces, city police, provincial police and R.C.M.P. in co-operation with the security forces of the United States and those of any other country where this man is likely to go must be brought into play, and everything that is humanly possible must be done at this time to bring him back into custody. I do not think it is good enough to be told today in the house that approximately four hours after the break was made the R.C.M.P. in Toronto were officially informed about it. I was in Toronto last night when this whole thing was taking place and returned on the 10.40 flight. Everybody knew about it because we heard about it when we reached Toronto airport and we also heard about it when we arrived at Ottawa airport. The newspaper people knew all about it because there were several of them at the Ottawa airport who were departing on the same flight to go to Montreal to cover the story. So I say that something certainly must be done to assure us and the Canadian people that the administration of justice and the keeping under detention of those who are charged with breaking the law are carried on more effectively.
I come back to the situation in the house this afternoon. We have laid aside the normal business of the house to discuss a matter of urgent public importance which you, Mr. Speaker, have recognized as such. Apparently this has been justified because there is concern in all parts of Canada regarding the carelessness of justice and law enforcement officials which has resulted in the escape from Bordeaux jail of Lucien Rivard. We are concerned that this should have taken place. More than that, I think the people of Canada are concerned about the whole matter of the integrity and honesty of people in public office, whether they are in this house, whether they are charged with the responsibility of law enforcement or charged with the responsibility of administering justice. We have read so much about this whole matter relating to bribery, coercion, dishonesty and moral laxity, because for months now it has made the headlines in our newspapers and has given genuine reason for everyone to be concerned.
It is also true that the government has a specific responsibility to clarify the charges that have been made at the earliest opportunity. They have not always done so, but it was for this reason that the Dorion inquiry was established and has now been conducting

Administration of Justice its investigations for several months. Because of the Dorion inquiry we are handicapped in demanding any debate in the house because we do not have the information which is necessary for us to debate the matter intelligently. It is good that the matter has come to the attention of the house in this way, that certain questions have been asked and that the responsibility in this matter is being pinned directly on the government and the Minister of Justice.
On the other hand, it is not good enough that we just take advantage of the opportunity for debate to carry on a show in the house because I do not think this will accomplish anything at all. This is the reason why we felt we were not justified in taking the time of the house to debate a matter about which we really did not have the necessary information, and could not obtain it because of the matter already being under consideration by the Dorion commission. I say it is not good enough to make the house even more of a political arena by trying to manoeuvre into a better tactical position. This is not good enough whether it is done by the Leader of the Opposition or whether, as the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) has said, an attempt is made to deal with other events which make the situation even more dirty and do not clarify the Rivard matter or clarify the situation in relation to the responsibility of the Dorion commission.
I agree that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) certainly has not been very fair nor maintained the standards he should have in trying to bring up a letter written some four years ago by the member for Brandon-Souris which was confidential and private and perhaps in the light of the circumstances did not have very much wrong with it. This is not why we are having this debate. The reason we are having the debate is to try to place a little more emphasis on the situation and, if possible, throw some light on the Rivard matter.

The second part of the motion before the house deals with the necessity for the broadening of the terms of reference of the Dorion inquiry to include an examination of all the sinister circumstances surrounding the disappearance of international narcotics criminal, Lucien Rivard. I think this is very important. I think it is the responsibility of the government to widen the terms of reference of the Dorion commission so that the fullest investigation and report can be made with regard to this whole matter. If the government does not do so it is again not facing up to its responsibility. That is why in my opinion the Minister of Justice should take heed of the second part of the motion.
I emphasize again that the Dorion commission must have its terms of reference broadened. As I understand the situation, there is no real problem in doing this. When the original terms of reference were spelled out on November 25 there was some discussion which resulted in the terms of reference being amended by the privy council on November 27. That amendment changed and broadened the terms of reference but I will not take the time now to place them on the record. I say this is necessary not only because of the new developments involved in the escape of Rivard and all its implications, but so that Mr. Justice Dorion can have the necessary authority to investigate in such a way as to bring the facts before the public. He has already told the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in a communication addressed directly to him that he does not have the authority in his present terms of reference to carry out the fullest investigation.
One of the things about which we have a great deal of reason to be concerned at this time is the work of our own security agencies. It is only a few days ago that I asked in the house whether or not the Minister of Justice would consider bringing in a white paper, or at least authorizing the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to publish certain information in regard to the security of this country, which would inform the Canadian people of what is taking place. We have too many instances in which there are subversive activities actually being carried on in this country which not only affect the security of this nation, but affect the security of the United States. If the security that is necessary for the R.C.M.P. to carry out its own responsibilities is not there, how can we expect to have a satisfactory situation so far as security in the country is concerned? It is for this reason there is a good deal of information that should be brought to light with regard to the very

breach of security that resulted in the appointment of the Dorion commission.
I respect the traditional right of all members of this house to not have their sources of information exposed. It is something that is absolutely essential if we are going to carry on our work in the proper way. On the other hand, if we cannot rely upon our own administration, whether it be in the Department of Justice or whether it be within the security forces themselves, then we do not have security in this country. In closing, therefore, I would urge the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister to take immediate action to broaden the terms of the Dorion commission so that commission can carry out the necessary investigation in its fullest aspects and bring to light every facet of the problem we are involved in discussing this afternoon.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.
The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) referred to my conduct in reading the letter from the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale).

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: You have just made a cowardly attack on him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I must say two things.
First, 1 am not the one who chose the date when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) moved the adjournment of the house. Furthermore, the tone of the debate was set not by myself but by the Leader of the Opposition.
The hon. member for Yukon did not say- and evidently will never say-that I made no comments regarding the conduct of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris who sent that letter. I merely read before this house a letter which is part of the public record and which was tabled in this house.
Furthermore, I said that neither the hon. member for Yukon nor the Leader of the Opposition would have dared to admit that, even if the situation was the same, the then minister of justice, when he decided to take action concerning this file, acted according to his conscience, and others must not be charged with less honest motives when in


even more favourable circumstances they endeavour to do their duty.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: They did not have $20,000.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I rise on a point of order. Whether or not there is a valid question of privilege affecting the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, that hon. member will have the opportunity of raising the matter at the first moment on his return to the house.
I rose to speak on the subject which the Leader of the Opposition and his colleagues were so anxious to discuss earlier this afternoon and this will be the only opportunity I shall have to speak on it. May I suggest that rather than be interrupted by all these questions of privilege I be allowed to proceed? As to the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur, if that is a proper question of privilege it should have been brought up at the earliest possible opportunity, that is at the commencement of the sitting. The hon. member did not do that and I therefore suggest there is no question of privilege before us.

speechtext: I want to give notice that I intend to move that this question be considered tomorrow during the orders of the day. subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: One blunder after another.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Tell that to the United States authorities.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: The United States authorities understand this perfectly well even though the hon. member may not. By a law of this parliament, the Extradition Act, it has been decided that the trial of persons against whom extradition is claimed shall be carried out in provincial courts. The constitution of Canada declares also that prisoners while awaiting trial are to be held in provincial prisons.

subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: "To be held"; note that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LAW ENFORCEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I would point out that this means it is the provincial institutions which have been given responsibility by this parliament for, first of all, trying the question of extradition and, second, for holding the person concerned while under trial.
The hon. member for Shefford has suggested that the federal government should authorize a royal commissioner under the federal Inquiries Act to inquire into the administration of justice by the provincial governments. This sounds very strange coming from the hon. member for Shefford; it sounds very strange coming from a colleague of the hon. member for Portneuf or the hon. member for Lake St. John to suggest there is anything wrong with the administration of justice by the authorities in Quebec.
